claim: The mean frequency of LFPs recorded in the stratum radiatum of CA1 was 45.2 ± 1.2 Hz in anesthetized rats (n = 7 animals).
source: The mean frequency of LFPs recorded in the stratum radiatum of CA1 was 45.2 ± 1.2 Hz (estimated from the autocorrelation function on 10 min epochs, n = 7 animals), which corresponds to the so-called low-gamma frequency band that characterizes the hippocampal segment under study (Csicsvari et al., 2003; Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2012a, 2012b; Martín-Vázquez et al., 2013; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct measurements from experimental data (autocorrelation function on 10 min epochs) and cites previous literature establishing this as the low-gamma frequency band.

claim: The mean frequency of 45.2 ± 1.2 Hz corresponds to the low-gamma frequency band that characterizes the hippocampal CA3-CA1 segment.
source: The mean frequency of LFPs recorded in the stratum radiatum of CA1 was 45.2 ± 1.2 Hz (estimated from the autocorrelation function on 10 min epochs, n = 7 animals), which corresponds to the so-called low-gamma frequency band that characterizes the hippocampal segment under study (Csicsvari et al., 2003; Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2012a, 2012b; Martín-Vázquez et al., 2013; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies that established this frequency range as low-gamma in the hippocampus.

claim: Bilateral excitatory Schaffer gamma waves are generally larger and lead from the right hemisphere.
source: Bilateral excitatory Schaffer gamma waves are generally larger and lead from the right hemisphere with only moderate covariation of amplitude, and drive CA1 pyramidal units more strongly than unilateral waves.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Bilateral Schaffer gamma waves drive CA1 pyramidal units more strongly than unilateral waves.
source: Bilateral excitatory Schaffer gamma waves are generally larger and lead from the right hemisphere with only moderate covariation of amplitude, and drive CA1 pyramidal units more strongly than unilateral waves.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data on unit firing presented in the results.

claim: CA3 waves lock to the ipsilateral Schaffer potentials.
source: CA3 waves lock to the ipsilateral Schaffer potentials, although bilateral coherence was weak.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data on temporal relationships between CA3som and Schaffer activities.

claim: Bilateral coherence of CA3 waves was weak.
source: CA3 waves lock to the ipsilateral Schaffer potentials, although bilateral coherence was weak.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract and supported by coherence analysis data in the results.

claim: Schaffer activity may run laterally after disruption of the connecting pathways.
source: Notably, Schaffer activity may run laterally, as seen after the disruption of the connecting pathways.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from lidocaine injection experiments.

claim: Asymmetric operations promote the entrainment of CA3-autonomous gamma oscillators bilaterally.
source: Thus, asymmetric operations promote the entrainment of CA3-autonomous gamma oscillators bilaterally, synchronizing lateralized gamma strings to converge optimally on CA1 targets.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the abstract, based on the observed asymmetric bilateral relationships.

claim: Interhippocampal connections integrate different aspects of information that flow through the left and right lobes.
source: The findings support the view that interhippocampal connections integrate different aspects of information that flow through the left and right lobes.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract, inferred from the experimental findings on bilateral integration.

claim: Lateralization of certain neural functions in vertebrates is thought to bear evolutionary advantages.
source: Lateralization of certain neural functions in vertebrates is thought to bear evolutionary advantages (Halpern et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on evolutionary advantages of lateralization.

claim: The bilateral function in the hippocampus is largely unknown.
source: The bilateral function in the hippocampus is largely unknown and it is unclear to what extent the two lobes convey similar or complementary information, and whether they do indeed work together.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, establishing the motivation for the study.

claim: Important bilateral connections exist between the same and different hippocampal subregions.
source: However, the existence of important bilateral connections between the same and different hippocampal subregions does suggest some degree of integration and cooperation.
evidence: This is a statement based on established anatomical knowledge of hippocampal connectivity.

claim: Hippocampal lateralization is observed during certain memory tasks in rodents.
source: In rodents, hippocampal lateralization is observed during certain memory tasks (Klur et al., 2009; Shipton et al., 2014), in the expression of synaptic plasticity (Kohl et al., 2011), or following environmental enrichment (Shinohara et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating lateralization in rodent hippocampus.

claim: Hippocampal lateralization is observed in the expression of synaptic plasticity in rodents.
source: In rodents, hippocampal lateralization is observed during certain memory tasks (Klur et al., 2009; Shipton et al., 2014), in the expression of synaptic plasticity (Kohl et al., 2011), or following environmental enrichment (Shinohara et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on synaptic plasticity.

claim: Hippocampal lateralization is observed following environmental enrichment in rodents.
source: In rodents, hippocampal lateralization is observed during certain memory tasks (Klur et al., 2009; Shipton et al., 2014), in the expression of synaptic plasticity (Kohl et al., 2011), or following environmental enrichment (Shinohara et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on environmental enrichment effects.

claim: Hippocampal lateralization was reported during sequence disambiguation in humans.
source: In the human, such lateralization was reported during sequence disambiguation (Kumaran and Maguire, 2006) and in cognitive navigation (Iaria et al., 2003; Iglói et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous human study.

claim: Hippocampal lateralization was reported in cognitive navigation in humans.
source: In the human, such lateralization was reported during sequence disambiguation (Kumaran and Maguire, 2006) and in cognitive navigation (Iaria et al., 2003; Iglói et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous human studies on navigation.

claim: The hippocampal CA3 region is an important hub for ascending and cortical pathways.
source: The hippocampal CA3 region is an important hub for ascending and cortical pathways (Vinogradova, 2001), and its output is conveyed to numerous brain regions, directly or from the next station in the CA1 after bilateral integration (Swanson et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on CA3 connectivity.

claim: CA3 output is conveyed to numerous brain regions, directly or from the CA1 after bilateral integration.
source: The hippocampal CA3 region is an important hub for ascending and cortical pathways (Vinogradova, 2001), and its output is conveyed to numerous brain regions, directly or from the next station in the CA1 after bilateral integration (Swanson et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on hippocampal output pathways.

claim: The left and right CA3 are connected reciprocally through the ventral hippocampal commissure (VHC).
source: The left and right CA3 are connected reciprocally through the ventral hippocampal commissure (VHC), and they also send excitatory inputs to the CA1 on both sides of the brain through an associational (Schaffer)-commissural system that converges on pyramidal cells (PCs, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: CA3 regions send excitatory inputs to the CA1 on both sides of the brain through an associational (Schaffer)-commissural system that converges on pyramidal cells.
source: The left and right CA3 are connected reciprocally through the ventral hippocampal commissure (VHC), and they also send excitatory inputs to the CA1 on both sides of the brain through an associational (Schaffer)-commissural system that converges on pyramidal cells (PCs, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The CA3 region behaves as a powerful gamma oscillator with inhibitory and excitatory local network components.
source: In addition, numerous electrophysiological studies show that the CA3 region behaves as a powerful gamma oscillator with inhibitory and excitatory local network components (Traub et al., 1996; Fisahn et al., 1998; Bartos et al., 2002; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Hájos et al., 2004; Mann et al., 2005; Oren et al., 2006; Hájos and Paulsen, 2009; Pietersen et al., 2009; Gulyás et al., 2010; Mann and Mody, 2010; Kohus et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: Significant wide band coherence exists between pairs of sites that are 0.5 mm apart within antero-posterior lamellar strips.
source: We found significant wide band coherence between pairs of sites that are 0.5 mm apart within antero-posterior (a-p) lamellar strips.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis of Schaffer activity.

claim: Coherence is reduced and restricted to the gamma band in bilateral comparisons.
source: This coherence is reduced and restricted to the gamma band in bilateral comparisons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The cross-correlation coefficient (CC) for La-Lp sites was 0.84 ± 0.03 (n = 7).
source: The cross-correlation coefficient (CC) behaved similarly (La-Lp, 0.84 ± 0.03; Ra-La, 0.57 ± 0.04; F(1,12) = 26.9; p<0.001; mean of epochs lasting 85–167 s, n = 7).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The cross-correlation coefficient (CC) for Ra-La sites was 0.57 ± 0.04 (n = 7).
source: The cross-correlation coefficient (CC) behaved similarly (La-Lp, 0.84 ± 0.03; Ra-La, 0.57 ± 0.04; F(1,12) = 26.9; p<0.001; mean of epochs lasting 85–167 s, n = 7).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The difference in cross-correlation coefficients between La-Lp and Ra-La comparisons is statistically significant (F(1,12) = 26.9; p<0.001).
source: The cross-correlation coefficient (CC) behaved similarly (La-Lp, 0.84 ± 0.03; Ra-La, 0.57 ± 0.04; F(1,12) = 26.9; p<0.001; mean of epochs lasting 85–167 s, n = 7).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The mean τmax of CCs was 0.32 ± 0.2 ms for a-p sites.
source: The mean τmax of CCs was similar for a-p sites (0.32 ± 0.2 ms) but shifted -0.82 ± 0.3 ms (F(1,12) = 8.5, p=0.01) for La-Ra comparisons, with the right side leading.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The mean τmax of CCs was -0.82 ± 0.3 ms for La-Ra comparisons, with the right side leading.
source: The mean τmax of CCs was similar for a-p sites (0.32 ± 0.2 ms) but shifted -0.82 ± 0.3 ms (F(1,12) = 8.5, p=0.01) for La-Ra comparisons, with the right side leading.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis indicating right-side precedence.

claim: Paired waves were nearly identical along lamellar strips in one side with amplitude covariance ρA = 0.78 ± 0.02 and duration covariance ρD = 0.63 ± 0.02 for La:Lp comparison.
source: Waves were designated as paired when they overlapped at two sites by at least 70% of their duration. Despite of a clear amplitude fluctuation at any site, paired waves were nearly identical along lamellar strips in one side (Figure 2A and B; covariance was ρA = 0.78 ± 0.02 for the amplitude and ρD = 0.63 ± 0.02 for the duration in La:Lp comparison), while they showed less co-variation between homotopic La-Ra sites (ρA = 0.5 ± 0.04 and ρD = 0.44 ± 0.03; see population statistics in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of individual gamma waves.

claim: Paired waves showed less co-variation between homotopic La-Ra sites with amplitude covariance ρA = 0.5 ± 0.04 and duration covariance ρD = 0.44 ± 0.03.
source: Waves were designated as paired when they overlapped at two sites by at least 70% of their duration. Despite of a clear amplitude fluctuation at any site, paired waves were nearly identical along lamellar strips in one side (Figure 2A and B; covariance was ρA = 0.78 ± 0.02 for the amplitude and ρD = 0.63 ± 0.02 for the duration in La:Lp comparison), while they showed less co-variation between homotopic La-Ra sites (ρA = 0.5 ± 0.04 and ρD = 0.44 ± 0.03; see population statistics in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of individual gamma waves.

claim: The mean wave duration was the same on both sides (R and L: 26.7 ± 0.7 ms; F(1,12) = 0, p=0.96).
source: The mean wave duration was the same on both sides (R and L: 26.7 ± 0.7 ms; F(1,12) = 0, p=0.96).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of individual gamma waves.

claim: Waves on the right side were larger in amplitude (Ra: 299 ± 11 µV; La: 237 ± 15 µV; F(1,12) = 12, p=0.005, n = 7 animals).
source: We found notable bilateral asymmetries. In particular, waves on the right side were larger in amplitude (Ra: 299 ± 11 µV; La: 237 ± 15 µV; F(1,12) = 12, p=0.005, n = 7 animals: Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of individual gamma waves showing bilateral asymmetry.

claim: Bilateral waves were rarely initiated synchronously.
source: Interestingly, bilateral waves were rarely initiated synchronously.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of wave timing.

claim: It was more common that waves in the right side led (55.6 ± 0.8% vs 44.4 ± 0.8%).
source: Although either side may lead (ovals in Figure 2C), it was more common that waves in the right side did so (55.6 ± 0.8% vs 44.4 ± 0.8% ).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of wave timing showing right-side precedence.

claim: On average, the R waves preceded with similar values between anterior or posterior sites (Ra-La: 0.62 ± 0.14 ms; Rp-Lp: 0.67 ± 0.18 ms).
source: On average, the R waves preceded with similar values between anterior or posterior sites (Ra-La: 0.62 ± 0.14 ms; Rp-Lp: 0.67 ± 0.18 ms).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of wave timing.

claim: A notable proportion of unilateral waves was found, with a higher incidence on the right side (R: 11.7 ± 2.4%; L: 5.5 ± 1%).
source: We also found a notable proportion of unilateral waves (Figure 2C), with a higher incidence on the right side (R: 11.7 ± 2.4%; L: 5.5 ± 1%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of wave occurrence.

claim: Unilateral waves were smaller than bilateral ones in the right hemisphere (212 ± 20 µV; bilateral vs. unilateral: p=0.002).
source: These unilateral waves were smaller than bilateral ones in the right hemisphere (212 ± 20 µV; bilateral vs. unilateral: p=0.002), but not in the left one (192 ± 20 µV; p=0.09).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of wave amplitudes.

claim: Unilateral waves in the left hemisphere were not significantly different in amplitude from bilateral ones (192 ± 20 µV; p=0.09).
source: These unilateral waves were smaller than bilateral ones in the right hemisphere (212 ± 20 µV; bilateral vs. unilateral: p=0.002), but not in the left one (192 ± 20 µV; p=0.09).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of wave amplitudes.

claim: The Granger Causality test confirmed statistically significant and reciprocal relations between the R and L sides (p=10–6 and p=10–8 for L to R and R to L relations, respectively).
source: The GC test confirmed that there are statistically significant and reciprocal relations between the R and L sides (Figure 3B: p=10–6 and p=10–8 for L to R and R to L relations, respectively).
evidence: This is a result from the Granger Causality statistical test applied to the data.

claim: The functional relation between R and L Schaffer activities peaked in the low-gamma frequency band (30–50 Hz) and the right to left link was strongly dominant over time.
source: Moreover, the functional relation peaked in the low-gamma frequency band (30–50 Hz) and the right to left link was strongly dominant over time (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is a result from the Granger Causality analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The mean phase lag between left and right Schaffer activities was 0.22 ± 0.04 radians, which is highly significant.
source: Figure 3E shows the histogram of the phases in Schaffer activity in the left side with onsets related to zero phases in the right side (corresponding to the beginning of LFP events in that side). The circular statistics confirmed the presence of a highly significant peak at Δϕ = 0.22 ± 0.04 radians.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phase shift analysis using circular statistics.

claim: The time lag corresponding to the phase shift of 0.22 ± 0.04 radians is Δt = 0.95 ± 0.2 ms.
source: By evaluating the mean frequency of the generators (~45 Hz) we can estimate the corresponding time lag Δt = 0.95 ± 0.2 ms, in a good agreement with the value obtained by the analysis of paired Schaffer waves (1.12 ms for this experiment).
evidence: This is a calculated result based on the phase shift and mean frequency of the generators.

claim: The mean phase lag across all seven animals was Δϕ = 0.12 ± 0.06 radians, corresponding to a time lag of Δt = 0.54 ± 0.26 ms.
source: Again this result was verified in all seven animals (Δϕ = 0.12 ± 0.06 radians; Δt = 0.54 ± 0.26 ms), with the mean time lag being roughly equal to the τmax in the CCs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phase shift analysis across all animals.

claim: The right-left lag was accentuated when R-waves were longer (a, p: 3.09 ± 0.06 and 3.03 ± 0.17 ms).
source: Notably, the right-left lag was accentuated when R-waves were longer (a, p: 3.09 ± 0.06 and 3.03 ± 0.17 ms), whilst longer L-waves also led to righ-hand ones albeit by a smaller amount (a, p: 1.97 ± 0.13 and 1.91 ± 0.23 ms, n = 7, F(1,12) = 517, p<0.001) (Figure 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of wave timing sorted by wave duration.

claim: Longer L-waves also led to right-hand ones albeit by a smaller amount (a, p: 1.97 ± 0.13 and 1.91 ± 0.23 ms, n = 7, F(1,12) = 517, p<0.001).
source: Notably, the right-left lag was accentuated when R-waves were longer (a, p: 3.09 ± 0.06 and 3.03 ± 0.17 ms), whilst longer L-waves also led to righ-hand ones albeit by a smaller amount (a, p: 1.97 ± 0.13 and 1.91 ± 0.23 ms, n = 7, F(1,12) = 517, p<0.001) (Figure 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of wave timing sorted by wave duration.

claim: There was a tendency towards a lead by longer and larger waves irrespective of the leading side.
source: We also found a tendency towards a lead by longer and larger waves irrespective of the leading side (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of wave features and timing.

claim: The minimum time used by CA3 spikes on one side to get to CA3 PCs on the other side through the VHC was 2.5 ± 0.1 ms (n = 6).
source: We explored this possibility by estimating the minimum time used by CA3 spikes on one side to get to CA3 PCs through the latency of the contralateral CA3 antidromic population spike elicited from the septal pole of the Left CA3, which was 2.5 ± 0.1 ms (n = 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from evoked potential measurements.

claim: The shortest possible lag for the direct driving of CA3 to the contralateral CA1 through the commissural pathway was 5.8 ± 0.3 ms (n = 7).
source: We also estimated the shortest possible lag for the direct driving of CA3 to the contralateral CA1 through the latency of the evoked commissural fEPSP in CA1, which amounted 5.8 ± 0.3 ms (n = 7, i.e.: three-fold the L-R lag for spontaneous paired waves).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from evoked potential measurements.

claim: On average Schaffer waves led in anterior sites (0.52 ± 0.06 and 0.67 ± 0.33 ms for the L and R sides, respectively; L-R: F(1,12) = 0.3, p=0.6).
source: Thus, while on average Schaffer waves led in anterior sites (0.52 ± 0.06 and 0.67 ± 0.33 ms for the L and R sides, respectively; L-R: F(1,12) = 0.3, p=0.6) in compliance with a global antero-posterior lamellar topology of Schaffer fibers, we found quite different lags depending on which a-p site had longer waves.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of antero-posterior wave timing.

claim: For waves that were longer in anterior sites the a-p lag increased to 2.6 ± 0.3 and 2.2 ± 0.3 ms in the right and left sides, respectively (R-L: F(1,12) = 0.65, p=0.4; total vs. longer R: F(1,12) = 102, p<0.001).
source: For waves that were longer in anterior sites the a-p lag increased to 2.6 ± 0.3 and 2.2 ± 0.3 ms in the right and left sides, respectively (R-L: F(1,12) = 0.65, p=0.4; total vs. longer R: F(1,12) = 102, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of antero-posterior wave timing sorted by wave duration.

claim: When posterior waves were longer they preceded anterior ones by 1.13 ± 0.5 and 1.8 ± 0.3 ms for the R and L sides, respectively (R-L: F(1,12) = 1.24, p=0.29; total vs. longer L: F(1,12) = 53, p<0.001).
source: More notably, when posterior waves were longer they preceded anterior ones by 1.13 ± 0.5 and 1.8 ± 0.3 ms for the R and L sides, respectively (R-L: F(1,12) = 1.24, p=0.29; total vs. longer L: F(1,12) = 53, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of antero-posterior wave timing sorted by wave duration.

claim: The CA3som generator is known to be part of a gamma pacemaker in the CA3 region.
source: This so-called the CA3som generator is known to be part of a gamma pacemaker in this region (Traub et al., 1996; Fisahn et al., 1998; Bartos et al., 2002; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Hájos et al., 2004; Mann et al., 2005; Oren et al., 2006; Hájos and Paulsen, 2009; Pietersen et al., 2009; Gulyás et al., 2010; Mann and Mody, 2010; Kohus et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on CA3 gamma oscillations.

claim: Unilateral CA3som waves occurred at 22 ± 1.2% on the left side and 26 ± 2.3% on the right side.
source: In order to compare the features of individual gamma waves and evaluate their synchronization at different sites, accurate determination of the waveforms is required (start time, amplitude and duration). Earlier we have used a wavelet transform method to detect short pulses (gamma waves) in the signal (Martín-Vázquez et al., 2015). However, we noticed that due to the frequent overlap of successive waves, the duration and the amplitude could be underestimated. Moreover, wk the starting time, which is essential in this study to explore bilateral synchronization, was only roughly approached. Here we implemented a new method using deconvolution of LFPs (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of CA3som wave occurrence.

claim: The antero-posterior wide band coherence of CA3som activity gave significant values for frequencies above 25 Hz in all cases.
source: Accordingly, the antero-posterior wide band coherence gave significant values for frequencies above 25 Hz in all cases, whilst none gave significant values for bilateral comparisons (Figure 4A, spectral coherence plots).
evidence: This is a result from the spectral coherence analysis of CA3som activity.

claim: Bilateral comparisons of CA3som activity gave no significant coherence values.
source: Accordingly, the antero-posterior wide band coherence gave significant values for frequencies above 25 Hz in all cases, whilst none gave significant values for bilateral comparisons (Figure 4A, spectral coherence plots).
evidence: This is a result from the spectral coherence analysis of CA3som activity.

claim: The cross-correlation coefficient for CA3som activity was 0.66 ± 0.6 for a-p comparisons and 0.27 ± 0.02 for L-R comparisons (F(1,12) = 32, p<0.001).
source: The CCs behaved similarly (a-p: 0.66 ± 0.6; L-R: 0.27 ± 0.02; F(1,12) = 32, p<0.001, with a non-significant phase difference between a-p comparisons (τmax: 0.1 ± 0.2 ms), but similar to Schaffer activity in R-L comparisons (0.42 ± 0.8 ms).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-correlation analysis of CA3som activity.

claim: The amplitude covariance of bilateral CA3som waves was stronger in intra (ρA = 0.62 ± 0.06) than interhippocampal waves (ρA = 0.24 ± 0.04; F(1,14) = 42, p<0.001).
source: Thus, the amplitude covariance of bilateral waves was stronger in intra (ρA = 0.62 ± 0.06) than interhippocampal waves (ρA = 0.24 ± 0.04; F(1,14) = 42, p<0.001), although the amplitude did not differ in the left and right hemispheres (La: 162 ± 26; Ra: 183 ± 28 μV; (F(1,10) = 0.32, p=0.58).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of CA3som wave amplitudes.

claim: The amplitude of CA3som waves did not differ in the left and right hemispheres (La: 162 ± 26; Ra: 183 ± 28 μV; F(1,10) = 0.32, p=0.58).
source: Thus, the amplitude covariance of bilateral waves was stronger in intra (ρA = 0.62 ± 0.06) than interhippocampal waves (ρA = 0.24 ± 0.04; F(1,14) = 42, p<0.001), although the amplitude did not differ in the left and right hemispheres (La: 162 ± 26; Ra: 183 ± 28 μV; (F(1,10) = 0.32, p=0.58).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of CA3som wave amplitudes.

claim: On average R-waves of CA3som led by 0.34 ± 0.1 ms (n = 8).
source: Also, on average R-waves led by 0.34 ± 0.1 ms (n = 8), and this lag increased to 2.72 ± 0.01 ms when the R-waves were longer (total vs. longer R: F(1,14) = 297, p<0.001), and longer L-waves also preceded the right-hand ones by 2.28 ± 0.02 ms (total vs. longer L: F(1,14) = 643, p<0.001; (Figure 2—source data 1), matching the relationships to the Schaffer waves.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of CA3som wave timing.

claim: The spectral coherence between CA3som and Schaffer activities was only significant in the gamma band in all cases.
source: Since we observed no differences between the sides and sites, we pooled the data from all shanks and animals where both activities could be recovered (n = 19). As expected from the flat baseline in the CA3som component, in all cases the spectral coherence between CA3som and Schaffer activities was only significant in the gamma band (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from the spectral coherence analysis between CA3som and Schaffer activities.

claim: The cross-correlation coefficient between CA3som and Schaffer activities was 0.4 ± 0.02, with τmax of 4.72 ± 0.4 ms.
source: Despite the tight temporal relationship between individual Schaffer and CA3som waves, the CC was only moderate (0.4 ± 0.02, τmax of 4.72 ± 0.4 ms), in part due to the different duration of the gamma waves (Schaffer waves are ~2.5 times longer than the CA3som ones and hence, the respective time courses are largely out-phased).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-correlation analysis between CA3som and Schaffer activities.

claim: The Granger Causality test indicated statistically significant reciprocal relationship between CA3som and Schaffer activities that peaked in the gamma frequency band, with the CA3som to Schaffer link strongly dominating.
source: We also applied the GC test to explore the relationship between the CA3som and Schaffer activities obtained at the same a-p site and side (two shanks on each of six animals: n = 12). In all cases, the GC test indicated statistically significant reciprocal relationship between the two activities that peaked in the gamma frequency band, and the CA3som to Schaffer link strongly dominated.
evidence: This is a result from the Granger Causality analysis between CA3som and Schaffer activities.

claim: The phase shift between CA3som and Schaffer activities yielded a highly significant peak at Δϕ = 1.46 ± 0.18 radians, with CA3som leading Schaffer activity.
source: We also evaluated the phase shift that yielded a highly significant peak at Δϕ = 1.46 ± 0.18 radians, the CA3som leading Schaffer activity.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phase shift analysis between CA3som and Schaffer activities.

claim: The estimated time lag between CA3som and Schaffer activities was Δt = 6.18 ± 0.7 ms, in good agreement with the τmax obtained from CCs.
source: The estimate time lag was Δt = 6.18 ± 0.7 ms, which is in a good agreement with the value of the τmax obtained from CCs.
evidence: This is a calculated result based on the phase shift and mean frequency.

claim: The amplitude co-variation between paired Schaffer and CA3som gamma waves was poor (ρA = 0.16 ± 0.02).
source: With regards to the features of extracted waves, the most relevant finding was the poor amplitude co-variation between paired Schaffer and CA3som gamma waves recorded by the same shank (ρA = 0.16 ± 0.02).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of paired wave amplitudes.

claim: The time lag between paired Schaffer and CA3som waves was not significant (0.12 ± 0.3 ms).
source: In addition, the time lag between paired Schaffer and CA3som waves was not significant (0.12 ± 0.3 ms), which should be interpreted in light of the different target cells and the reduced sampling (42.3 ± 2% of CA3som waves remained unpaired).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of paired wave timing.

claim: 42.3 ± 2% of CA3som waves remained unpaired with Schaffer waves.
source: In addition, the time lag between paired Schaffer and CA3som waves was not significant (0.12 ± 0.3 ms), which should be interpreted in light of the different target cells and the reduced sampling (42.3 ± 2% of CA3som waves remained unpaired).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of wave pairing.

claim: CA1 pyramidal cells fired preferentially upon convergence of bilateral gamma waves.
source: PCs fired preferentially upon convergence of bilateral gamma waves, while putative interneurons showed a marked unilateral drive.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of unit firing in relation to gamma waves, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Putative interneurons showed a marked unilateral drive.
source: PCs fired preferentially upon convergence of bilateral gamma waves, while putative interneurons showed a marked unilateral drive.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of unit firing in relation to gamma waves, shown in Figure 5.

claim: A large proportion of putative CA1 interneurons showed tight phase-locked firing shortly after the start of the bilateral gamma waves.
source: In turn, a large proportion of putative CA1 interneurons showed tight phase-locked firing shortly after the start of the bilateral gamma waves, and they also fired more frequently than PCs in response to unilateral waves on the same side (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of interneuron firing patterns shown in the figures.

claim: Putative interneurons fired more frequently than PCs in response to unilateral waves on the same side.
source: In turn, a large proportion of putative CA1 interneurons showed tight phase-locked firing shortly after the start of the bilateral gamma waves, and they also fired more frequently than PCs in response to unilateral waves on the same side (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of unit firing patterns shown in the figures.

claim: The coincidence of left-hand and right-hand waves (bilateral excitation) plays crucial role in PC firing, while the associated power increase has a marginal effect.
source: Thus, the coincidence of left-hand and right-hand waves (i.e.: bilateral excitation) plays crucial role in PC firing, while the associated power increase has a marginal effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of PC firing probability versus Schaffer power shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Following lidocaine injection in the VHC, Schaffer gamma strings were still observed bilaterally, but frequent unilateral strings occurred that were not seen in the controls.
source: Notably, although Schaffer gamma strings were still observed bilaterally, frequent unilateral strings occurred that were not seen in the controls (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the VHC disruption experiment shown in the figures.

claim: After VHC disruption, the overall power and wave characteristics on either side did not change.
source: When they co-occurred we found that the overall power and wave characteristics on either side did not change (Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), evidence that each CA3 can autonomously generate gamma in vivo, as reported earlier for chemically-induced gamma oscillations in vitro (Oren et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from the VHC disruption experiment shown in the figures.

claim: Each CA3 can autonomously generate gamma in vivo.
source: When they co-occurred we found that the overall power and wave characteristics on either side did not change (Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), evidence that each CA3 can autonomously generate gamma in vivo, as reported earlier for chemically-induced gamma oscillations in vitro (Oren et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference from the VHC disruption experiment, supported by citation to previous in vitro work.

claim: After VHC disruption, coarse bilateral co-modulation was maintained, albeit reduced (CC, 0.62 ± 0.03 vs 0.45 ± 0.05; p=0.007; n = 4 animals).
source: Coarse bilateral co-modulation was maintained, albeit reduced (CC, 0.62 ± 0.03 vs 0.45 ± 0.05; p=0.007; mean of epochs lasting 100 s in n = 4 animals; Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the VHC disruption experiment.

claim: After VHC disruption, bilateral gamma coherence was lost.
source: Moreover, bilateral gamma coherence was lost (Figure 6F and Figure 6—source data 1) and consequently, the L-R synchrony of individual gamma waves disappeared while the amplitude variability of the waves remained high in both sides (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the VHC disruption experiment shown in the figures.

claim: After VHC disruption, the L-R synchrony of individual gamma waves disappeared while the amplitude variability of the waves remained high in both sides.
source: Moreover, bilateral gamma coherence was lost (Figure 6F and Figure 6—source data 1) and consequently, the L-R synchrony of individual gamma waves disappeared while the amplitude variability of the waves remained high in both sides (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the VHC disruption experiment shown in the figures.

claim: Different gamma strings may circulate independently through L and R hippocampi after VHC disruption.
source: This indicates that different gamma strings may circulate independently through L and R hippocampi.
evidence: This is an inference from the VHC disruption experiment results.

claim: The Granger Causality test indicates that Schaffer activity on any side may predict activity on the other, and the R-to-L influence is more robust.
source: The GC test indicates that Schaffer activity on any side may predict activity on the other, and the R-to-L influence is more robust.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the Granger Causality analysis discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The primacy of the right lobe is supported by evidence from the extracted waves: (a) the mean lag between paired bilateral waves shows quantitative advance on the right-hand side (around 0.6–0.8 ms); (b) The mean amplitude of Schaffer waves was 30% larger on the right-hand side; (c) CA3som waves showed a similar advance on the right-hand side; (d) The cumulated lag in crossed comparisons, either summed (Lp-Ra) or balanced (La-Rp), in consonance with the partial lags between a-p and R-L sites.
source: In a strict sense, the primacy of the right lobe is supported by evidence from the extracted waves, which can be considered discrete events independent from each other: (a) the mean lag between paired bilateral waves shows quantitative advance on the right-hand side (around 0.6–0.8 ms); (b) The mean amplitude of Schaffer waves was 30% larger on the right-hand side; (c) CA3som waves showed a similar advance on the right-hand side; (d) The cumulated lag in crossed comparisons, either summed (Lp-Ra) or balanced (La-Rp), in consonance with the partial lags between a-p and R-L sites.
evidence: This is a summary of multiple lines of evidence supporting right-side primacy, discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The short mean lag between paired bilateral waves indicates that the system is finely adjusted to optimize the temporal overlap of excitatory envelopes from both sides.
source: Since the fate of a Schaffer wave is to excite CA1 units where it integrates with input from the contralateral side it is crucial to optimize the temporal overlap of the respective excitatory envelopes. Therefore, the short mean lag between paired bilateral waves indicates that the system is so finely adjusted (see functional implications below).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The minimum time required for CA3 spikes to reach contralateral CA3 PCs is 2.5 ms, which when added to the time required for synaptic integration and assembly recruitment is insufficient to explain the lag in the majority of paired waves.
source: For instance if PC assemblies are recruited through the so-called leader PC cells (Fujisawa et al., 2006; Wittner and Miles, 2007), the driving factor between such cells may require shorter lags. On the other hand, a direct contralateral driving of gamma waves in the CA1 via commissural fibers is less likely for several reasons: (a) the minimum lag of commissural evoked potentials is already in the higher range of the lags between spontaneous bilateral waves; (b) the commissural pathway contributes little to field potentials due to anatomical and geometrical factors (Martín-Vázquez et al., 2015), making gamma waves of such origin unlikely; (c) the presence of unilateral waves coincides on the same idea, i.e., since a CA3 assembly may initiate a Schaffer wave that has no contralateral counterpart, when contralateral waves appear they most likely have an ipsilateral origin; (d) finally, the disruption of the VHC, or the unilateral inactivation of the CA3 would markedly reduce the presence of Schaffer waves and dampen the mean power of the Schaffer generator, which does not happen.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data and evoked potential measurements, discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: A direct contralateral driving of gamma waves in the CA1 via commissural fibers is less likely based on multiple lines of evidence.
source: On the other hand, a direct contralateral driving of gamma waves in the CA1 via commissural fibers is less likely for several reasons: (a) the minimum lag of commissural evoked potentials is already in the higher range of the lags between spontaneous bilateral waves; (b) the commissural pathway contributes little to field potentials due to anatomical and geometrical factors (Martín-Vázquez et al., 2015), making gamma waves of such origin unlikely; (c) the presence of unilateral waves coincides on the same idea, i.e., since a CA3 assembly may initiate a Schaffer wave that has no contralateral counterpart, when contralateral waves appear they most likely have an ipsilateral origin; (d) finally, the disruption of the VHC, or the unilateral inactivation of the CA3 would markedly reduce the presence of Schaffer waves and dampen the mean power of the Schaffer generator, which does not happen.
evidence: This is an inference from multiple lines of experimental evidence, discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The most likely origin of bilateral Schaffer waves is an independent ipsilateral driving.
source: Therefore, although unilateral CA3 assemblies driving contralateral ones cannot be ruled out entirely, the most likely origin is an independent ipsilateral driving.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of multiple lines of evidence, discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: Once every gamma cycle a collection of spatial modules of the CA1 dendritic space is activated over the septo-temporal axis by multiple independent CA3 assemblies with either a dominant lamellar or longitudinal projection, converging with others entering from the contralateral side.
source: The emerging view (Figure 7) is that once every gamma cycle a collection of spatial modules of the CA1 dendritic space is activated over the septo-temporal axis by multiple independent CA3 assemblies with either a dominant lamellar or longitudinal projection, converging with others entering from the contralateral side.
evidence: This is a conceptual model synthesized from the experimental findings, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The CA3som gamma wavelets are tightly locked to ipsilateral Schaffer waves.
source: Instead, the CA3som gamma wavelets are tightly locked to ipsilateral Schaffer waves.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of CA3som and Schaffer relationships, discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The CA3som waves arise from basket cell-mediated recurrent inhibition following CA3 PC firing.
source: We should have in account that the Schaffer waves are detected in CA1 recordings ~2–3 ms after CA3 PCs fire, a lag that is fully compatible with CA3som waves arising from basket cell-mediated recurrent inhibition following the same PC firing (Hájos et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the timing relationships, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The CA3som activity participates mainly in ipsilateral mechanisms.
source: All these findings support a main participation of the CA3som activity in ipsilateral mechanisms, as also indicated by the large ipsilateral coherence and the nearly synchronous occurrence of waves at anterior and posterior sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of CA3som bilateral relationships, discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The nearly synchronous occurrence of CA3som waves at anterior and posterior sites is consistent with the reported coupling of activity in subnetworks of inhibitory cells.
source: This latter feature is consistent with the reported coupling of activity in subnetworks of inhibitory cells (Galarreta and Hestrin, 1999; Tamás et al., 2000), which provides modulation of CA3 output over extended domains.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by citations to previous work on inhibitory cell coupling.

claim: The strikingly poor covariation between CA3som and Schaffer waves does not appear to be in consonance with the view that somatic inhibitory input plays a role in selecting the CA3 domain of PC cells from which the functional assembly forming a Schaffer wave arises.
source: On another line, one might think that a somatic inhibitory input plays a role in selecting the CA3 domain of PC cells from which the functional assembly forming a Schaffer wave arises. However, the strikingly poor covariation between CA3som and Schaffer waves does not appear to be in consonance with this view.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental finding of poor amplitude covariation, discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: Multiple CA3 assemblies may share a common domain, since nearby PC cells rarely fire together.
source: Another possibility is that multiple CA3 assemblies share a common domain, since nearby PC cells rarely fire together (Takahashi et al., 2010; Matsumoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis discussed in the Discussion section, supported by citations to previous studies on PC firing patterns.

claim: Both CA3 PCs and basket cells may receive a common tonic input that codes for the duration of the gamma strings and intermissions, possibly as an energy-saving mechanism.
source: A possible explanation of this is that both CA3 PCs and basket cells receive a common tonic input (Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006; Freund and Katona, 2007) that codes for the duration of the gamma strings and intermissions, possibly as an energy-saving mechanism to stop the intrinsic oscillators in absence of activity and when bilateral entrainment is unnecessary.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis discussed in the Discussion section, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Gamma oscillations form rapidly from small clusters of interconnected cells.
source: Theoretical studies show that gamma oscillations form rapidly from small clusters of interconnected cells (Börgers et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a theoretical study.

claim: Coding is optimized by global oscillations within a population whose units fire sparsely.
source: Indeed, coding is optimized by global oscillations within a population whose units fire sparsely (Engel et al., 2001; Fries, 2009; Chalk et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: The gamma rhythmic CA3 input implies some sort of chunked information.
source: From the side of target CA1 units, the gamma rhythmic CA3 input implies some sort of chunked information, as recently proposed in the cortex (Hyafil et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of gamma oscillations, supported by a citation to a recent proposal.

claim: In some epochs the information conveyed is similar on both sides and it differs in others.
source: This observation already indicates that in some epochs the information conveyed is similar on both sides and it differs in others, which is also supported by the bilateral out-phasing of gamma waves and the occurrence of some unilateral gamma strings upon VHC disruption.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations of bilateral covariation and VHC disruption effects.

claim: The blockade of the contralateral CA3 input modifies the firing rate of units but the changes were balanced at the population level.
source: Curiously, the blockade of the contralateral CA3 input modifies the firing rate of units but the changes were balanced at the population level, in agreement with previous findings (Zemankovics et al., 2013; Middleton and McHugh, 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the CA3 blockade experiment, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The two CA3-originated excitations summed in CA1 units do not operate as a simple integrator, but rather the output is defined on a single cell basis in concert with other inputs.
source: In the context of bilateral integration, we may then infer that the two CA3-originated excitations summed in CA1 units do not operate as a simple integrator, but rather the output is defined on a single cell basis in concert with other inputs, such as that from inhibitory neurons that are also modulated by interhippocampal disruption.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings on unit firing and bilateral integration.

claim: The rather disperse firing of PCs over the gamma cycle may arise from the slower dynamics of intracellular EPSPs compared to EPSCs and/or the variable influence of different interneuron subtypes with distinct phase coupling to gamma waves.
source: Such dispersion may arise from the slower dynamics of intracellular EPSPs compared to EPSCs (reflected in extracellular field waves), and/or the variable influence of different interneuron subtypes with distinct phase coupling to gamma waves (Hájos et al., 2004; Tukker et al., 2007; Vinck et al., 2010; Varga et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed dispersion of PC firing, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some interneurons can be envisaged as timing devices for different inputs to converge at optimal instants.
source: Indeed some interneurons can be envisaged as timing devices for different inputs to converge at optimal instants.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional role of interneurons.

claim: The gamma-phase shifting of CA1-PCs is in contrast with the tight gamma coupling of CA3-PCs, indicating a short-lived gamma pattern restricted to the CA3-CA1 segment of the hippocampal circuit.
source: In turn, the gamma-phase shifting of CA1-PCs is in contrast with the tight gamma coupling of CA3-PCs (Hájos et al., 2004; Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2012a), indicating a short-lived gamma pattern restricted to this segment of the hippocampal circuit.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of CA3 and CA1 PC firing patterns, supported by citations.

claim: No gamma pattern was found in the subicular projection of the CA1 population.
source: Indeed, we have not found a gamma pattern in the subicular projection of the CA1 population (Makarova and Herreras, unpublished results).
evidence: This is a statement about unpublished observations.

claim: Connection asymmetry favors temporal association.
source: Theoretical studies indicate that connection asymmetry favors temporal association (Sompolinsky and Kanter, 1986) and the generation of robust transients of sequential activation (Rabinovich et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: The dominance of the right side of the CA3 may constitute a physiological mechanism to provide a fast dynamic trade-off between left and right CA3 gamma oscillators for the fast bilateral synchronization and stabilization of the entrainment of autonomous CA3 gamma oscillators.
source: The dominance of the right side of the CA3 may thus constitute a physiological mechanism to provide a fast dynamic trade-off between left and right CA3 gamma oscillators for the fast bilateral synchronization and stabilization of the entrainment of autonomous CA3 gamma oscillators despite of the strong amplitude variability of individual waves.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional significance of right-side dominance, inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The main functional role for CA3 gamma oscillations is their bilateral entrainment, rather than transmitting gamma activity to the cortex.
source: Overall, the present observations are compatible with the hypothesis that the main functional role for CA3 gamma oscillations is their bilateral entrainment, rather than transmitting gamma activity to the cortex.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional role of CA3 gamma oscillations, inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The larger Schaffer waves in the right-hand side may reflect left-right asymmetry in the subunit composition of Glutamate receptors reported in the CA1.
source: The larger Schaffer waves in the right-hand side may reflect left-right asymmetry in the subunit composition of Glutamate receptors reported in the CA1 (Kawakami et al., 2003; Shinohara et al., 2008), although a larger size of CA3 assemblies on the right-hand side cannot be excluded.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed amplitude asymmetry, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Right dominance better fits a hardware-like role to promote the integration of lateralized streams of information.
source: In addition, right dominance better fits a hardware-like role to promote the integration of lateralized streams of information, but we cannot rule the priority or the qualitative relevance of that running through the left and right circuits during specific tasks (Klur et al., 2009; Shinohara et al., 2013; Shipton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of right dominance, with acknowledgment of alternative possibilities supported by citations.

claim: Different hippocampal subregions are known to be differentially involved in the encoding and consolidation/retrieval of spatial information.
source: Different hippocampal subregions are known to be differentially involved in the encoding and consolidation/retrieval of spatial information (Jerman et al., 2006; Hunsaker et al., 2008), or in perceived versus reconstructed scenes (Zeidman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spatial and non-spatial information converge in the hippocampus to form episodic memories.
source: Also, spatial and non-spatial information converge in the hippocampus to form episodic memories (Leutgeb et al., 2004), although functional difference between hemispheres has rarely been invoked.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Both CA3 are required for short-term memory, yet only inactivation of the left CA3 impairs performance in an associative spatial long-term memory task and plasticity.
source: A significant finding is that both CA3 are required for short-term memory, yet only inactivation of the left CA3 impairs performance in an associative spatial long-term memory task and plasticity (Shipton et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The left and right sides do not convey equivalent information.
source: Along with the present observations of independent gamma strings upon VHC blockade, it becomes clear that the left and right sides do not convey equivalent information.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental findings on VHC blockade and previous literature.

claim: The hippocampus is thought to represent behavioral episodes as sequences of events.
source: The hippocampus is thought to represent behavioral episodes as sequences of events (Eichenbaum, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous theoretical framework.

claim: Groups of CA3 assemblies distributed over the septotemporal axis may sequentially code the relevant features of a scene in a gamma string, which are checked against each other bilaterally to form higher order features and to modulate parallel or lateralized output to the cortex.
source: Based on the assembly code of CA3-transmitted activity, one interesting possibility is that groups of CA3 assemblies distributed over the septotemporal axis (Benito et al., 2014) sequentially code the relevant features of a scene in a gamma string, which are checked against each other bilaterally to form higher order features and to modulate parallel or lateralized output to the cortex (Ciocchi et al., 2015) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the functional role of bilateral CA3 assemblies, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The simplicity of the bilateral integration mechanism makes likely that it subserves bilateral assemblage of lateralized activity in other brain structures.
source: The simplicity of this mechanism makes likely that it subserves bilateral assemblage of lateralized activity in other brain structures.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization of the findings to other brain structures.
